truth.city: Jerash (Wadi Al-Deir / Al-Rayyan area, west of city centre)

coarse_filters.approx_climate_biome: Mediterranean semi-arid highlands; olive groves, limestone hills, dry pale soils

cues.observation: All commercial signage is Modern Standard Arabic with Levantine shop conventions ('مفروشات', 'مطعم'), plus bilingual Arabic/English lines ('Supermarket', 'Adam & Kenan market').
Advertised mobile numbers begin with 077 / 079 (0779885566, 0791519494, 0779644224) — the Jordanian Zain/Umniah/Orange mobile prefix pattern.
A building-materials shop is named 'إعمار جرش للمواد البناء' — 'I'mar Jerash', explicitly naming Jerash as the local business identity.
Shawarma sign carries the sub-brand line 'وادي الدير' (Wadi al-Deir), a locality name found in the Jerash/Ajloun hill country.
Buildings are faced with rough-dressed pale limestone ('Jordanian white stone') over concrete frames, with unfinished rebar columns on roofs for future floors.
Large blue polyethylene roof water tanks plus a black tank — standard Jordanian intermittent-supply water storage; Israeli/settlement roofs would show black tanks with solar collectors instead.
Terraced olive groves on chalky hillsides with scattered pine; classic 700-1000 m northwest Jordanian highland landscape rather than desert plateau.
Dense white cubic housing spreading over several hilltops across a valley, with a small commercial strip on the through-road — a large village/small town, not a city core.
Vehicles keep to the right; sedans are older Japanese/Korean models typical of Jordanian second-hand fleets.
Pharmacy, decor shop, mini-market and imported-goods stores with Coca-Cola/Pepsi coolers; Sunni Arab small-town consumer economy, no Hebrew or Latin-script municipal signage.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A Sunni Arab highland town of modest but stable means: family-owned shawarma joints, furniture/carpet dealers, building-materials and car-detailing shops serving a self-build housing economy. Roof rebar left standing for later floors and rooftop water tanks indicate incremental construction and intermittent municipal water. Bilingual Arabic/English branding with Latin-script vanity names ('Baker Street', 'Azad Clean', 'Modern Style') shows aspirational small-business marketing typical of Jordan's provincial towns rather than the capital.

ruled_out: Eastern desert: no olive terraces there
Jordan Valley: wrong crops and elevation

narrowing.discriminator: An Ajloun or Irbid trade name would more typically read 'إعمار عجلون' or reference Irbid; local hardware suppliers brand with their own governorate seat. The presence of 'Jerash' in a builders' merchant name, plus the 'Wadi al-Deir' locality tag, points to the Jerash catchment rather than Ajloun town or the Irbid plain (which is flatter, wheat-dominated, and more urban).
narrowing.observation: 'I'mar Jerash' building-materials shop and a shawarma brand tagged 'Wadi al-Deir'.
ruled_out: Ajloun: no Ajloun toponym in signage; forest cover would be denser oak/pine
Irbid plain: terrain here is steep valley-and-ridge, not open arable plateau

narrowing.conclusion: A hillside village/small town on the road network around Jerash, most likely in the Wadi al-Deir / Sakib direction
narrowing.discriminator: Jerash town centre would have visible Roman ruins, tourist signage, hotel/souvenir shops and wider paved boulevards; here the strip is a single two-lane through-road with unpaved shoulders, roadside merchandise displays and olive groves reaching the pavement — a village edge.
narrowing.observation: One narrow through-road, gravel forecourts, goods stacked outside the shop, olive trees directly adjoining the commercial frontage, no tourist infrastructure.
ruled_out: Jerash town centre: no antiquities, tourist signage or urban kerbing

coarse_filters.approx_climate_biome: Eastern Mediterranean semi-arid highland; olive terraces on limestone hills, dry summer

cues.observation: All signage in Arabic with occasional English transliteration ('Adam & Kenan market', 'Baker Street Shawarma'); no French, no Hebrew, no Turkish Latin letters.
Building-supply shop named 'I'mar Jarash' (Jerash Construction Materials) — a locality-branded business.
Cream/beige limestone-clad multi-storey houses with exposed rebar columns on the roof for future floors, plus blue polyethylene rooftop water tanks.
Dense olive groves on terraced limestone slopes, green hills in the background, no palms or red sandstone.
White/cream cubic houses scattered across successive hill ridges of a broad valley — classic Irbid–Jerash–Ajloun highland village sprawl.
Olive terraces dominate with no pine forest cover visible on the surrounding ridges.
Right-hand traffic, unmarked worn asphalt, wooden/concrete utility poles with low-hanging overhead lines, no sidewalks in places.
Ground-floor arcade of stone-clad building with pharmacy, supermarket, decor and cosmetics shops — small-town commercial spine rather than city centre.
Mostly older Japanese/Korean sedans and a light-blue minibus typical of Jordanian rural public transport.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: Sunni Arab Levantine highland town, lower-middle income. Economy is a mix of small retail and services (shawarma stands, furniture, dry-cleaning, building materials, pharmacy) plus olive agriculture on the terraces. Incremental owner-built stone-clad housing with protruding rebar and universal rooftop water tanks signals limited capital, self-financed construction, and intermittent municipal water. English used decoratively on shopfronts (an aspirational branding cue) rather than functionally; WhatsApp numbers as the main contact channel indicate an informal, mobile-first commercial sector.

Irbid's plateau villages are flatter with wider grain/olive fields and fewer deep valley cuts. Salt/Balqa would show its distinctive dense Ottoman-era yellow-limestone terraced townscape. The building-supply store branded 'I'mar Jarash' points to a business trading on the Jerash name, typical of shops in or immediately around that governorate.
narrowing.observation: Pure olive-terrace hillsides with no pine cover; a construction-materials shop explicitly named 'Jarash'; a deeply incised valley with villages on facing ridges.
ruled_out: Ajloun — no pine forest on the ridges

correction.summary: HIT: Jordan / Jerash Governorate / western Jerash outskirts (Wadi Al-Deir) confirmed with 2.6 km error. The decisive chain was Arabic-only signage with English (not French/Hebrew) as second language, recurring 077x/079x mobile prefixes on shop fascias, cream limestone cladding with rooftop rebar and blue polyethylene water tanks, and terraced olive hillsides without pine cover. Syria and the West Bank were correctly excluded by phone-prefix format, building material and the absence of Hebrew/political iconography; Ajloun was excluded by the pure olive terracing with no Aleppo-pine ridgelines.

misleading_cues.observation: Absence of Roman ruins, tourist signage or civic buildings led to the conclusion that this must be a village well away from the governorate seat.
misleading_cues.why_misleading: In hilly Jordanian towns the archaeological core is often only 2-3 km away and completely hidden behind ridges; a purely local shop ribbon with olive groves at the back can still be an outskirt neighbourhood of the seat itself, not a separate village.

misleading_cues.observation: The 'Wadi al-Deir' text on one shawarma sign was read only as a generic brand.
misleading_cues.why_misleading: Locality names printed under a brand ('وادي الدير') are usually the actual neighbourhood, a stronger pinpoint than the reasoning about village-vs-town morphology.

decisive_cues.observation: Six independent shop fascias carry mobile numbers beginning 0776/0778/0779/0791.
decisive_cues.why_decisive: This prefix block is Jordan-specific; Syria (093/094), West Bank (059/056) and Lebanon (03/70/71) would look different, so it locks the country without any other cue.

decisive_cues.observation: Multi-storey houses clad in cream/beige limestone slabs, with rebar columns protruding from flat roofs and blue polyethylene water tanks on top.
decisive_cues.why_decisive: Cream limestone cladding plus incremental self-build and rooftop tanks is the standard Jordanian highland housing typology, unlike grey bare block in Syria or red brick in Egypt.

decisive_cues.observation: Terraced olive groves on pale limestone slopes, green in low winter sun, villages spread over facing ridges of a dissected valley.
decisive_cues.why_decisive: Places the pano in the Irbid–Jerash–Ajloun olive belt rather than the treeless southern steppe or desert Jordan.

decisive_cues.observation: No pine or conifer cover on any ridgeline, only olives; deeply incised valley rather than open plateau.
decisive_cues.why_decisive: Separates Jerash-area valley slopes from higher Ajloun (Aleppo pine) and from the flatter Irbid plateau.

decisive_cues.observation: Shop names in pure Arabic with English transliteration only ('Adam & Kenan market', 'Modern Style', 'Azad Clean'), no French and no Hebrew.
decisive_cues.why_decisive: Excludes Lebanon/Maghreb (French) and mixed Israeli/West Bank areas (Hebrew traces).

discriminators.title: Jordan vs Syria: mobile prefixes and facade material on shop signs
discriminators.body: In Jordan almost every shop fascia advertises a mobile number starting 077x or 079x, and buildings are faced with sawn cream limestone slabs. In Syria you would instead read 093x/094x/098x numbers and see largely unrendered grey concrete-block or plaster facades with far less stone cladding.

discriminators.title: Jordan vs West Bank: prefixes, iconography and Street View coverage
discriminators.body: Jordanian highland strips show 077x/079x numbers, no political murals and continuous official Street View. In the Palestinian West Bank you would instead see 059x/056x numbers, frequent Palestinian flags, martyr posters or faction murals, plus patchy/unofficial coverage and occasional Hebrew or Israeli-plate vehicles.

discriminators.title: Jerash valley slopes vs Ajloun ridges: pure olive terrace vs pine mix
discriminators.body: Around Jerash the dissected limestone valleys are covered almost exclusively in terraced olive groves with bare rocky interfluves. In Ajloun, only ~20 km west and several hundred metres higher, you would instead see Aleppo pine and oak woodland capping the ridgelines above the olives.

discriminators.title: Absence of ruins does not exclude the governorate seat in hilly Jordan
discriminators.body: In Jordan's ridge-and-valley north, the outskirts of a governorate seat look like a plain shop ribbon of furniture, dry-cleaning and building-supply stores with olive groves behind and no sidewalks, because the historic/tourist core sits in a separate wadi 2-3 km away and is invisible. Do not downgrade to 'distant village' on missing monuments alone; instead use neighbourhood names printed on shop signs, which typically name the actual quarter of the town.

discriminators.title: Jordanian incremental stone self-build vs Egyptian red brick
discriminators.body: Jordanian towns show three- to four-storey family houses clad in cream limestone with rebar stubs on the flat roof and blue plastic water tanks. In Egypt you would instead see unrendered red-brick frames with no stone cladding and mostly galvanised or black tanks, alongside 010/011/012 phone prefixes.
